title: Drive-tunable Floquet exchange spectroscopy with Hong--Ou--Mandel interference
abstract: Floquet driving reshapes cavity spectra, but single-photon sideband populations do not reveal how it changes two-photon exchange. Here we show theoretically that delay-resolved Hong--Ou--Mandel (HOM) coincidences can probe this response in a collectively coupled cavity. A frequency-entangled signal photon scatters linearly from the driven cavity while its idler provides a delayed reference. Averaging over an unsynchronized drive phase removes coherence between different net output orders but preserves exchange interference within each order. Fourier transformation of the coincidence trace yields two drive-dependent exchange branches associated with the Floquet-polariton spectrum. As the drive changes, the branches shift and exchange weight; the dominant physical output order also changes, a transfer not reproduced by single-photon sideband populations. We further map the coincidence-trace response over drive frequency and amplitude and connect it to a count-model-dependent Fisher information. Floquet control thus adds a tunable exchange spectrum to HOM interferometry and gives quantitative targets for an experiment.
summary: This paper theoretically shows how periodic driving (Floquet engineering) can be used to control and spectroscopically map the two-photon exchange response in a cavity QED system using Hong-Ou-Mandel interference. By analyzing the coincidence rate, the authors reveal tunable exchange branches that provide a richer diagnostic tool than traditional single-photon measurements. This establishes a pathway for actively programming the coincidence spectrum in quantum optical experiments.
main_problem: The study aims to probe how Floquet driving modifies the two-photon exchange response in a cavity system, a feature not accessible by measuring single-photon sideband populations alone.
main_result: The research demonstrates that Floquet driving allows for the spectral tuning of the two-photon exchange spectrum, shifting characteristic branches and changing the dominant output order in a way that single-photon measurements cannot replicate.
method: The authors theoretically model the system using delay-resolved Hong-Ou-Mandel (HOM) coincidences, analyzing the coincidence rate after Fourier transforming the delay-domain signal.
model_or_system: The system is a collectively coupled cavity, modeled using the Tavis-Cummings framework and subjected to periodic Floquet driving. The analysis involves solving a tridiagonal system describing the cavity field amplitude in the frequency domain.
key_observables: Delay-resolved Hong-Ou-Mandel (HOM) coincidences, which yield two drive-dependent exchange branches in the Fourier spectrum, and a count-model-dependent Fisher information metric.
important_parameters: Drive frequency ($\Omega$), drive amplitude ($A$), cavity detuning, and the time delay ($	au$) between the signal and idler photons.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes weak excitation, a single-mode homogeneous collective bright mode, and that the cavity acts linearly on the signal photon, with the two-photon observable arising from final-stage interference.
figures_summary: Figure 1 proposes the HOM spectroscopy setup. Figure 2 shows the delay-domain and drive-frequency dependence of the biphoton probe. Figure 4 illustrates the predicted HOM response metric over the drive controls ($\Omega, A$).
paper_structure: The paper establishes the theoretical framework for using HOM interference to measure two-photon exchange. It derives the necessary equations for the coincidence probability, analyzes the spectral features resulting from the drive, and finally maps the tunability using response metrics.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant to AMO physics and quantum optics as it demonstrates a powerful, non-linear control mechanism (Floquet driving) to engineer and spectroscopically map complex quantum correlations (two-photon exchange) in cavity QED systems.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Proposed HOM spectroscopy of a Floquet Tavis– Cummings cavity. An SPDC source generates a frequency- entangled signal–idler pair. The signal traverses a collectively coupled cavity–emitter system with cavity frequency modu- lated as ωc(t) = ωc + A sin(Ωt), while the idler acquires a controllable delay τ. Coincidences after the balanced beam splitter measure the exchange overlap of the outgoing pho- tons.

FIG. 2. Delay-domain and drive-frequency dependence of the same biphoton probe. (a) Conditional HOM interferograms with no cavity, a bare cavity, and a static Tavis–Cummings cavity (A = 0). (b) Phase-averaged conditional coincidence P c(τ, Ω) for the Tavis–Cummings cavity as a function of idler delay and positive drive frequency 0.2 ≤Ω/κ ≤5. The unmodulated Ω= 0 response is shown in (a) and is omitted from the lower map. We use A/κ = 2.385 and the drive convention A sin(Ωt). The color scale is the absolute coincidence probability. The dashed line marks the static polariton splitting ∆pol from Eq. (16).

FIG. 3. Drive-tunable Floquet exchange spectrum at fixed A/κ = 2.385. (a) Magnitude of the Fourier transform of P c(τ)−1/2 versus drive frequency Ωand exchange-beat frequency ν. White markers track the two dominant complementary branches; the vertical dotted line marks the static polariton splitting ∆pol. (b) Selected spectra show the drive-dependent transfer of exchange weight between the branches.

FIG. 4. Predicted HOM response metric over drive controls (Ω, A). The diagonal components measure the integrated trace response to each control; gΩA measures their alignment, and det g the squared area spanned by the two local responses. The cross in panel (c) marks (Ω, A)/κ = (2.2, 2.385), selected for the phase-sensitive controls in the Supplemental Material.
